plan.topic: Threw up after the big holiday dinner on tirzepatide? What the label says about vomiting, fluids and when to call
plan.angle: Tirzepatide and vomiting after a big meal: the label lists vomiting as a common side effect (rounded top dose vs placebo from Zepbound PI Table 2, with the population on screen). Separate label fact: it slows stomach emptying. Untagged, guilt-free tips: sip fluids little and often unless you've been told to limit fluids, and wait for hunger to come back. Contact your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down or feel dizzy or are passing very little urine, because fluid loss has been linked to kidney problems. Emergency card: severe stomach pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting, means stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. Then the exact fixed don't-stop line, without 'keep to your usual schedule'. Then the low-blood-sugar line scoped to insulin or a sulfonylurea and adults without type 2 diabetes, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide: Threw Up After the Big Dinner? #shorts
plan.why: The playbook gives the 20:00 slot to the holiday table through 11-27. 'Still full the morning after' got 513 views. Vomiting after the big meal is a new felt moment we haven't covered in the last 30 days. | fact-check: The label-based angle is fine. The Zepbound Medication Guide pancreatitis line ('stop using and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting') and the dehydration and kidney warning both fit. Fixes: (1) Drop 'keep to your usual schedule' from the don't-stop line. After a vomiting episode that reads as dosing or schedule advice. Use the fixed line exactly: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' (2) Keep the framing guilt-free. The hook must not suggest overeating 'caused' the vomiting or that the viewer did something wrong. (3) Say the gastric-emptying sentence as a label fact, not as the cause of this episode (no 'so', and no 'that's why'). (4) Give the vomiting rate as the label's rounded top-dose vs placebo figure, with the Table 2 population (adults in the label's weight-management trials, as printed) on screen. (5) Add signs of dehydration (dizziness, very little urine) to the 'contact your prescriber' trigger, since you can't keep fluids down. Keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'. (6) The low-blood-sugar line must say it's higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea and is also reported in adults without type 2 diabetes.

script.cta: Spoken ending: "Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber." This is one on-screen card ending in a full stop. Then the loop line "Remember the number?", which leads back into sentence 1. No subscribe line and no "link in the description". Spoken count: 119 words (120 if "stomach-emptying" counts as two), inside the tight arm of 90–120. Post notes (Exp G): the watch-next target is the Thanksgiving long video (holiday Short → Thanksgiving), and the publisher adds the verified link. Source note: in s04, zep-pi and zep-mg support only "Dehydration may cause kidney problems." The trigger question ("Can't keep fluids down, dizzy, or peeing little?") and "Contact your prescriber" are an untagged channel help line.

factcheck.summary: The facts check out against the current Zepbound label on DailyMed, revised 28 Aug 2026. Table 1 shows vomiting at 13% on 15 mg vs 2% on placebo. Those figures are pooled from Studies 1 and 2 (adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks). Section 12.2 says the delay in stomach emptying "diminishes over time". Section 5.7 says low blood sugar has also been linked to the drug in adults without type 2 diabetes. Section 5.3 covers acute kidney injury from fluid loss. The Medication Guide says dehydration may cause kidney problems. The pancreatitis line uses the tirzepatide wording ("with or without vomiting") and keeps "right away". The don't-stop line uses the single-sign form, and the fluid caveat is there. The safety line is one card ending in a full stop. The Short is 119 spoken words (my count), so it fits the tight arm. There is no subscribe line and no "link in the description" line. Four small fixes remain: the stat card's population drops "weight-related", the s03 card's wording can be misread, the title implies a link to big meals that the content never covers, and the hypoglycemia section number is missing from the source title. The Medication Guide and PI PDFs exist at their URLs, but their text couldn't be read through the fetcher. I checked the PI wording on DailyMed and confirmed the Medication Guide's dehydration sentence through search.
